periods.public: The participants introduce their priorities for the investigation. They focus on historical data, staffing levels, financial commitments, and operational bottlenecks.

lines.May: Suggests looking at old pilots and accessibility records to avoid repeating mistakes.
lines.Benjamin: Proposes checking roster books and crew establishment to ensure feasibility.
lines.Midori: Requests timed runs and journey audits to identify real delays.
lines.Shizue: Wants to see joint committee minutes and contingency pricing for old structures.
lines.Jonathan: Suggests capital ledger balances and ticketing contractor fees.

lines.May: Agrees with the need for operational data.
lines.Benjamin: Asks if others agree on the importance of staffing.
lines.Midori: Supports the focus on passenger experience.
lines.Shizue: Emphasizes the risk of hidden physical obstacles.
lines.Jonathan: Notes the importance of long-term financial obligations.

periods.public: Participants share the implications of their findings without revealing the specific candidates yet. They discuss the tension between staffing shortages, financial leaks, and infrastructure risks.

lines.May: Mentions that some past trials were actually successful and some infrastructure projects failed.
lines.Benjamin: Warns that the late-turn pool and general crew levels are dangerously low.
lines.Midori: Points out that waiting for connections is the main time-sink, not the travel itself.
lines.Shizue: Notes that inter-agency agreement is lacking and old shells are risky.
lines.Jonathan: Highlights that contractor fees are eating into the paving budget.

lines.May: Asks @Benjamin if staffing affects all types of expansion.
lines.Benjamin: Confirms that overnight work and late shifts are particularly strained.
lines.Midori: Questions if the ticketing system is actually the cause of the delays.
lines.Shizue: Expresses concern over the lack of consensus between operators.
lines.Jonathan: Mentions a ring-fenced balance that might be usable.

lines.May: Observes that some technical trials from years ago were sound.
lines.Benjamin: Notes that maintenance contracts for certain equipment actually have capacity.
lines.Midori: Argues against fixing things that aren't the primary cause of delay.
lines.Shizue: Warns against projects requiring heavy coordination with uncooperative partners.
lines.Jonathan: Questions the sustainability of current contractor fee structures.

periods.public: The candidates are revealed. The group evaluates them against the discovered constraints: staffing, inter-agency cooperation, financial sustainability, and actual passenger needs.

lines.May: Advocates for the fare system based on the successful old pilot.
lines.Benjamin: Supports the station upgrades because the maintenance contract has capacity.
lines.Midori: Agrees with the station upgrades to improve passenger flow.
lines.Shizue: Favors station upgrades as they avoid the inter-agency deadlock of other plans.
lines.Jonathan: Leans toward the fare system to stop the drain of multiple contractor fees.

lines.May: Argues that the fare system is a low-risk win based on history.
lines.Benjamin: Objects to the night extension due to the depleted late-turn pool.
lines.Midori: Questions the utility of the bus corridor if the issue is connections.
lines.Shizue: Warns that the bus corridor requires roadway consents that might be tricky.
lines.Jonathan: Asks @Benjamin if station upgrades would stress the crew too much.

lines.May: Tries to convince the others that the fare system is the most efficient.
lines.Benjamin: Reassures @Jonathan that the specific maintenance capacity makes station upgrades viable.
lines.Midori: Agrees that station upgrades address the movement issues.
lines.Shizue: Confirms that station upgrades are the safest bet for delivery.
lines.Jonathan: Acknowledges the logic but remains interested in the financial fix.

lines.May: Accepts the consensus but maintains her preference.
lines.Benjamin: Ready to vote for the most feasible option.
lines.Midori: Ready to vote for the passenger-centric option.
lines.Shizue: Ready to vote for the most deliverable option.
lines.Jonathan: Ready to vote for the most fiscally sound option.

seats.Jonathan: Cares about long-term financial commitments and contractor costs. He argues from a fiscal perspective and remains cautious about future liabilities.
seats.Shizue: Cares about delivery risks and bureaucratic hurdles. She argues for the path of least resistance regarding approvals and physical surprises.
seats.May: Cares about institutional memory and past failures/successes. She argues based on historical evidence and closure reports.
seats.Midori: Cares about actual passenger time-loss versus perceived crowding. She argues for data-driven improvements to the passenger journey.
seats.Benjamin: Cares about staffing levels and the burden on crews. He argues based on the practical availability of personnel to execute the plan.
